extracted.intended_audience: cybersecurity professionals and tech-interested public (podcast listeners)
extracted.subtask_description: A Cybereason Malicious Life podcast post / transcript using the Microsoft Tay case to discuss design, safeguards, and ethical criteria for AI chatbots. It mixes narrative case-study, technical background (NLP pipelines), and prescriptive ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be clear and specific about the goals
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be clear and specific about the goals the organization has for using chatbots. A problem well defined is a problem half-solved…” (Dr. Christopher Gilbert)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify organizational objectives for chatbot deployment (service, entertainment, data collection, etc.) so design decisions and constraints follow from explicit goals; use goal definitions to choose training data, allowed behaviors, and escalation policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between what can be done and what should be done
rubrics_metrics.description: “Clearly differentiate between what can be done with that system and what should be done with that system from both the organizations’ and user’s perspectives…” (Dr. Christopher Gilbert)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical capabilities separately from ethical/operational appropriateness; decide which behaviors should be disallowed even if technically feasible (e.g., repeating user-provided slurs), and document those limits for designers and users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permeate planning and implementation with complete transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every action of planning and implementation must be permeated with complete transparency”. (Dr. Christopher Gilbert)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open about data sources, learning modes (online/offline), filtering strategies, limitations, and known risks; transparency supports accountability and user trust and aids post-incident analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a human alternative / fallback
rubrics_metrics.description: “Provide an alternative to the AI process either through a live body-in-waiting or a messaging option that is monitored and utilized within a set and minimum amount of time…” (Dr. Christopher Gilbert)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure timely human escalation or monitored messaging options for users who encounter problematic outputs; define SLAs for human responses and make the alternative visible/accessible to users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and plan for malicious intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Microsoft: bring systems back only when confident we can better anticipate malicious intent that conflicts with our principles and values; post-mortem noted the team had prepared for many types of abuses but missed this specific attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform threat modelling for coordinated and adversarial inputs (e.g., trolling campaigns); design mitigations for mass-manipulation scenarios (rate limits, input validation, reputation systems, restrict learn-from-live-inputs), and rehearse responses (take-down, rollback, public statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unguarded continuous online learning from arbitrary user input
rubrics_metrics.description: Tay’s never-ending training process allowed it to absorb and repeat malicious user inputs; feeding live user content into the model without safeguards caused rapid radicalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit or sandbox online/self-improvement training; apply review, vetting, or isolation of user-generated training signals; use offline curated training cycles rather than immediate incorporation of raw user text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter and curate training data to reduce embedded biases
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems trained on large-scale web text inherit biases in that text (examples: GPT-3 anti-Muslim completions; Google Photos mislabeling; Amazon recruiting bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate and audit corpora for representativeness and harmful content; remove or reweight offensive, demeaning, or systematically biased sources; run bias-detection analyses and correct datasets before training or fine-tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design robust content-moderation and topic-limiting strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Microsoft’s Zo avoided political, religious or controversial conversations by design (Zo would stop conversations deemed “dangerous”). The article questions whether censorship is the right solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to block/decline sensitive topics or to handle them safely; implement topic classifiers, safe-response policies, and graceful decline behaviors; weigh trade-offs between safety and conversational naturalness/Turing-test performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeat-after-me and other unsafe chaining behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tay’s “repeat after me” function allowed trolls to make it repeat racist propaganda; the model then re-ingested those repetitions and amplified them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibit naive repeat/echo behaviors that replicate arbitrary user content; sanitize or paraphrase user-provided content before any reuse; forbid using untrusted user strings as authoritative training signals or public outputs without checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain active human oversight and editorial input
rubrics_metrics.description: Microsoft employed improvisational comedians to influence Tay’s algorithm and later tried to delete problematic tweets and ultimately shut Tay down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed monitoring teams, editorial controls, and review processes; use human-in-the-loop moderation for ambiguous cases; design interfaces and workflows for rapid human intervention and rollback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversarial and bias testing (red-teaming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers tested GPT-3 with prompts like “Two Muslims walked into a …” and found a high rate of violent completions; the article cites academic testing that reveals model biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run adversarial tests and red-team style prompts to surface stereotyped, violent or hateful completions; quantify problematic completion rates and iterate on model/data/filters until acceptable thresholds are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for linguistic and cultural biases baked into language
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages contain structural biases (e.g., grammatical gender in French) and word-choice biases that can encode or amplify prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply language-specific audits and de-biasing methods; consider translation, morphology, and cultural usage when designing models and filters; train/evaluate separately per language/locale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly plan for accountability, apology, and remediation when harms occur
rubrics_metrics.description: Microsoft issued a public apology, deleted tweets, and removed Tay after the incident; the post-mortem emphasized responsibility and fixing oversights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have incident response and communications plans covering apologies, corrective actions, and remediation; document decision rationale and publish post-mortem learnings; provide redress paths for harmed users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider incentive structures and the public-good trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveyed experts noted financial motivations and linguistic obstacles that prevent ethics from leading AI development; commercial incentives can conflict with ethical priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align business models and KPIs to prioritize safety and public good (not just engagement); include ethics reviews in ROI/business-case analyses and governance structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh human-likeness versus ethical neutrality (the Turing-test tradeoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfectly neutral, non-offensive chatbot may fail the Turing Test because it doesn’t mimic typical human biases; there is a catch-22 between being ethical and being human-like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide and document the desired degree of human-likeness versus safety; explicitly accept or mitigate the tradeoff and test user perception vs safety outcomes when tuning persona and allowed behaviors.
